title: Shepherds, Humility, and Standing Firm
summary: Peter charges elders to shepherd God’s flock, calls the whole church to humility and watchfulness, and closes with assurance of God’s restoring grace.
historicalContext: The churches of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia were scattered groups of believers facing slander, social exclusion, and the threat of harsher treatment for the name of Christ. Leadership in such congregations rested with elders, a title inherited from Israel’s synagogue life and applied in the apostolic churches to those who oversaw local believers. In a world where authority usually meant status, patronage, and the right to command, Peter writes from the imperial capital he calls “Babylon,” sharing his readers’ exile. Silvanus, long a trusted companion of the apostles, carries the letter, and Mark, once a deserter on a missionary journey and now a restored coworker, adds his greeting. The apostle who would soon die for his Lord writes as a fellow sufferer to leaders and members who must hold together under pressure without either surrendering their witness or turning on one another.
literaryContext: Chapter 5 completes the letter’s long exhortation on suffering for doing good. Having said that judgment begins at the house of God (4:17), Peter turns to those responsible for that house: elders are to shepherd as Christ did, and the whole flock is to put on humility. The shepherd language recalls 2:25, where Christ is the Shepherd and Bishop of souls, and the promise of a crown of glory echoes the unfading inheritance of 1:4. The commands to humble oneself, cast care on God, be sober, and resist the devil gather earlier threads (1:13; 4:7, 19) into a final call to steadfastness. Verses 10–11 answer the opening blessing of 1:3–7 with a promise and doxology, while the greetings of verses 12–14 mirror the address of 1:1–2: the elect sojourners of the dispersion are greeted by the church elect together with them in Babylon.
themes: Shepherd leadership under the Chief Shepherd
Humility toward one another and before God
Entrusting every anxiety to a caring Father
Watchful resistance in the great controversy
Glory after a little while of suffering
Standing fast in the true grace of God

outline.title: Shepherds of God’s Flock
outline.summary: Peter, as fellow elder and witness, charges the elders to tend the flock willingly, eagerly, and by example, looking for the crown the Chief Shepherd will give at His appearing.

outline.title: Clothed with Humility
outline.summary: The younger are to submit to the elders, all are to wear humility toward one another, and every believer is to bow under God’s mighty hand and cast all care upon Him.

outline.title: Resisting the Adversary, Kept by Grace
outline.summary: Believers must stay sober and watchful against the devil, resist him firm in the faith, and rest in the God of all grace who will perfect and establish them.

outline.title: Final Testimony and Greetings
outline.summary: Peter commends Silvanus, affirms that his message is the true grace of God, and sends greetings from Babylon with a closing word of love and peace.

verses.bibleText: The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word “elders” follows naturally from the warning that judgment begins at the house of God (4:17). If the household is being tested, those who care for it carry special responsibility. In the apostolic churches elders were the recognized leaders of local congregations, a title rooted in Israel’s history and carried into the church from its earliest days (Acts 11:30; 14:23). Peter does not command them from a distance. “I exhort” translates a verb of earnest appeal, the language of a friend who comes alongside rather than a superior issuing orders.

His self-description is striking. Though an apostle (1:1), he calls himself a “fellow elder,” standing on the same level as the leaders he addresses. He claims no rank over them, only shared labor. The man who once argued with others over who would be greatest has learned the lesson of the towel and basin. Whatever authority he carries flows from his service to Christ, and he calls the elders into that same service.

Peter is also “a witness of the sufferings of Christ.” He had heard Jesus foretell the cross, watched the agony in Gethsemane, and followed at a distance into the high priest’s courtyard. His testimony rests on what he saw. Yet witnessing also means bearing testimony, and Peter’s own life of faithful leadership under threat continues that witness. The elders who lead in dangerous times join him in it.

Finally, he is “a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed.” Suffering and glory belong together in this letter (1:11; 4:13). Peter already shares in the coming glory by promise, though its unveiling awaits Christ’s return. This hope steadies both him and the elders. The path of service may lead through hardship, as Jesus had told Peter it would (John 21:18–19), but it ends in the revealing of glory that no persecutor can take away.

wordNotes.term: ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος (ho sympresbyteros) — who am also an elder
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the fellow elder,” a compound found only here in the New Testament. The prefix expresses partnership: Peter places himself alongside the elders rather than above them. The word reflects solidarity in labor and danger, and it fits the pattern in which apostles shared leadership with local elders (Acts 15:6).

One who shares in something with others, a partner. Peter speaks of sharing in glory not yet revealed, treating the future as so certain that he can describe himself as already a participant. The same word family describes believers as sharers in Christ’s sufferings (4:13) and in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

verses.bibleText: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Feed the flock of God” carries a charge Peter himself once received. Beside the Sea of Galilee the risen Lord asked him three times whether he loved Him, and three times gave him the care of His sheep (John 21:15–17). The verb means more than providing food. It covers everything a shepherd does: leading, guarding, gathering strays, binding the injured, and keeping watch at night. Peter now passes that commission on to the elders of Asia Minor.

The flock is “of God.” It does not belong to the elders, the congregation, or any human institution. That ownership both dignifies and limits their work. They tend what God has purchased (Acts 20:28), and they will answer to Him for how they treated His people. Ezekiel’s indictment of Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves and ruled the sheep with force, stands behind Peter’s words (Ezekiel 34:2–4). God promised to raise up shepherds after His own heart, and Peter calls the elders to be such men.

“Taking the oversight” translates a verb related to the word for overseer, used of Christ Himself in 2:25. In the New Testament elders and overseers describe the same leaders from different angles: the one stresses maturity, the other the work of watching over others.

Peter then sets out how this oversight is to be done, in a series of contrasts. First, “not by constraint, but willingly.” A leader who serves only because no one else would or because he feels trapped will serve poorly. Some manuscripts add “according to God,” suggesting that willing service matches God’s own way of caring for His people. Second, “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind.” Workers may receive support (1 Corinthians 9:14), yet the prospect of gain must never be the motive. The phrase points to shameful profit, the temptation to turn ministry into a source of personal advantage. Its opposite is eagerness, a readiness to give oneself that does not calculate return. In communities under financial and social pressure, leaders who served for gain would soon abandon the flock when the cost rose.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to act as a shepherd: to tend, protect, guide, and nourish a flock. It is the same command Jesus gave Peter in John 21:16. The image describes leadership as care for the well-being of others, modeled on God as the Shepherd of Israel.

An adverb found only here in the New Testament, describing an eagerness for shameful or dishonest profit. Related words appear in the qualifications for church leaders, who must not be greedy of base gain. The concern is motive and integrity, not whether a minister may be supported.

verses.bibleText: Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third contrast reaches the heart of Christian leadership: “neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.” The verb for lording it over is the very word Jesus used when He described the rulers of the Gentiles, who exercise dominion over their subjects (Mark 10:42). Among His followers, He said, it would not be so. Greatness would be measured by service, and the model would be the Son of Man who came to give His life. Peter, who heard those words firsthand, now applies them to the elders.

“Heritage” renders a word for an allotted portion. The believers under each elder’s care have been assigned to him, as an inheritance was once distributed by lot in Israel. That allotment calls for gratitude and accountability, never for possession.

The alternative to domination is example. Elders lead by living the faith they teach, giving the flock a pattern it can safely follow. Authority that rests on example persuades; authority that rests on force only compels. Paul likewise urged believers to follow him as he followed Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). In a suffering church, an elder who endures reproach patiently, forgives freely, and keeps doing good teaches more than many instructions could.

wordNotes.explanation: To exercise lordship over others, often with the sense of domineering or subduing them. Jesus used the word for pagan rulers whose style His disciples must reject. Peter forbids elders to treat the people entrusted to them as subjects to be controlled.

A typos was an impression or pattern, the mark left by a stamp or the model for a copy. Leaders are to be living patterns of the Christian life that others may imitate. Paul uses the same word for himself and for Timothy and Titus.

verses.bibleText: And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when the chief Shepherd shall appear” lifts the eyes of weary leaders to the day that makes their labor worthwhile. Jesus is the Chief Shepherd, the One over all under-shepherds. He called Himself the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Hebrews calls Him the great Shepherd brought again from the dead (Hebrews 13:20). Elders shepherd on His behalf; they are accountable to Him and depend on Him. The flock remains His, and He alone can finally keep it.

The timing of the reward matters. Peter does not say elders receive their crown at death but “when the chief Shepherd shall appear.” The reward is linked to the visible return of Christ, the same revelation of glory mentioned in verse 1 and throughout the letter (1:7, 13; 4:13). Faithful servants who die before that day rest in the grave until the resurrection, and then all receive their reward together (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Peter, who knew he would soon lay aside his earthly tent (2 Peter 1:14), placed his own hope in that same appearing.

“A crown of glory that fadeth not away” contrasts sharply with the wreaths of leaves given to winners in ancient games, which withered within days. The crown is glory itself, or a crown consisting of glory, and it will never wilt. Many elders in Peter’s day received no honor from their neighbors, only suspicion and abuse. Some would lose property or life. Christ promises a recognition that outlasts every earthly honor.

The Bible does not shy away from reward as a motive for faithful service. Jesus spoke of treasure in heaven and of a full reward for those who suffer for His name (Matthew 5:12). Such reward does not earn salvation, which is entirely of grace. It expresses the Lord’s delight in acknowledging those who served His flock for His sake, and it frees leaders from needing applause now.

wordNotes.explanation: A compound of “chief” and “shepherd,” used only here in the New Testament as a title of Christ. It describes the head shepherd who oversees all who tend the flock. Elders serve under Him and answer to Him, and the title echoes God’s promise to shepherd His scattered people Himself.

wordNotes.term: τὸν ἀμαράντινον τῆς δόξης στέφανον (ton amarantinon tēs doxēs stephanon) — a crown of glory that fadeth not away
wordNotes.explanation: The stephanos was a victor’s wreath, not a royal diadem. The adjective “amaranthine” describes something that does not wither, recalling the unfading inheritance of 1:4. The image promises lasting honor at Christ’s appearing, in contrast to perishable earthly glory.

verses.bibleText: Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder.” Having told the elders how to lead, Peter turns to those they lead. The word “likewise” ties this instruction to the charge just given: as elders serve under the Chief Shepherd, the rest of the flock is to accept the care of its shepherds. “Younger” may refer to those younger in years, who in any ancient community were expected to respect their seniors. In this context, however, it most likely includes all who are not elders, those newer to the faith and less experienced in its demands. The term “elder” here naturally carries both senses, age and office, since leaders were usually chosen from the mature.

Submission in this letter is never servile. Peter has used the same verb for citizens before rulers (2:13), servants before masters (2:18), and wives toward husbands (3:1), and in each case it describes a voluntary ordering of oneself for the Lord’s sake. Here it means teachable respect for those who watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17), following the example they set (v. 3). It does not mean surrendering conscience, for the elders themselves have just been forbidden to dominate.

Then Peter widens the circle: “Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility.” Leaders and members alike are to wear humility. The verb pictures tying on a garment, perhaps the apron a servant wore while working. Peter may have remembered the evening when Jesus girded Himself with a towel and washed the disciples’ feet, Peter’s among them (John 13:4–5). Humility is to be put on deliberately and kept on, so that it becomes the visible mark of every believer.

The reason is drawn from Proverbs 3:34: “God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.” James quotes the same text (James 4:6). The verb “resisteth” is military, describing an army drawn up in battle formation against an enemy. Pride sets a person against God Himself. Arrogant leaders who domineer and arrogant members who scorn guidance both find God opposing them. To the humble, by contrast, He gives grace, the very favor and strength they need to endure. In a church under pressure, where fear can make leaders harsh and members rebellious, this shared humility keeps the community together.

wordNotes.explanation: A rare verb meaning to tie or fasten something on oneself. It may suggest the apron of a servant, worn while doing humble work. Whether or not that specific garment is in view, the picture is of humility deliberately put on and fixed in place as the believer’s working clothes.

The verb means to set oneself in array against, as troops are ranged for battle. Quoting Proverbs 3:34, Peter teaches that pride is more than a social flaw; it places a person in opposition to God, while humility opens the way to His grace.

verses.bibleText: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Humility toward one another now becomes humility before God. “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God.” The phrase “mighty hand” comes from the story of the Exodus, where it describes the power by which God brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:19–20; Deuteronomy 26:8). The same hand that disciplines also delivers. To humble oneself under it is to accept God’s present dealings, including the hardships that come because one belongs to Christ, without bitterness against Him or retaliation against others.

For Peter’s readers, humiliation was already a reality. They had lost standing among neighbors and family by confessing Christ. The question was how they would respond: by resenting their lowered position, by trying to win back honor through compromise, or by trusting God’s hand. Peter calls them to the third.

The purpose is “that he may exalt you in due time.” Jesus taught that whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), and He Himself walked that road from the cross to the right hand of God. Believers follow the same pattern. The exaltation comes “in due time,” at the season God has appointed, which in this letter points above all to the revelation of Jesus Christ. Waiting for that time is part of humility; the humble do not try to seize their vindication early.

wordNotes.term: τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ (tēn krataian cheira tou theou) — the mighty hand of God
wordNotes.explanation: An expression drawn from the Exodus narratives, where God’s mighty hand both judged Egypt and delivered His people. In Peter’s use it reminds believers that their present trials lie within the reach of the same power that redeemed Israel.

wordNotes.term: ἐν καιρῷ (en kairō) — in due time
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in season,” the right or appointed time. The phrase stresses that God determines when the humble will be lifted up. In 1 Peter that moment centers on Christ’s appearing, though God may also honor faithfulness earlier.

verses.bibleText: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” The grammar links this verse closely to the previous one: humbling oneself under God’s hand is carried out by casting one’s anxieties on Him. Pride insists on carrying its own burdens, imagining that everything depends on its own vigilance. Humility admits weakness and hands the load to God.

Peter echoes Psalm 55:22, where David, betrayed by a close friend, tells himself to cast his burden on the Lord. The verb is vivid: to throw something onto another. It appears elsewhere for throwing garments onto a colt for Jesus to ride (Luke 19:35). Believers are to throw their worries onto God rather than keep turning them over in their hands. The word “all” leaves nothing out, whether fear of persecution, loss of livelihood, family strain, or concern for the future.

The ground of this act is God’s personal concern: “he careth for you.” On a storm-tossed sea the disciples once cried, “Master, carest thou not that we perish?” (Mark 4:38). Peter, who was in that boat, now answers the question. God does care, and nothing His children face escapes His notice. Jesus taught the same lesson with sparrows and the hairs of the head (Matthew 10:29–31). Anxiety handed over in this way leaves the mind clear for the watchfulness Peter is about to demand, since a heart consumed by worry has little attention left for the enemy at the door.

wordNotes.explanation: Anxiety or worry, the kind of concern that divides and distracts the mind. Jesus warned that the cares of this world choke the word (Mark 4:19) and told His followers not to be anxious. Peter directs believers to place every such burden on God.

wordNotes.term: αὐτῷ μέλει περὶ ὑμῶν (autō melei peri hymōn) — he careth for you
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “it matters to him concerning you.” The expression stresses God’s personal interest in His people. The same verb is used in the disciples’ question in the storm, which this assurance answers.

verses.bibleText: Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Freedom from anxiety does not mean carelessness. “Be sober, be vigilant” are two sharp commands with no connecting word, like a sentry’s warning. Sobriety means a clear, self-controlled mind, free from the confusion of drunkenness and of runaway desire (1:13; 4:7). Vigilance means staying awake and alert. Peter knew the cost of failing here. In Gethsemane Jesus had urged him to watch and pray, and he fell asleep three times; that same night he denied his Lord (Mark 14:37–38, 66–72). Jesus had also warned him that Satan desired to sift him as wheat (Luke 22:31). The apostle speaks from bitter experience.

The reason for alertness is a real enemy: “your adversary the devil.” “Adversary” was a word for an opponent in a lawsuit, and “devil” means slanderer or accuser. The two titles fit together, for Scripture depicts Satan as the accuser of the brethren (Revelation 12:10) and as the one who brought charges against Job (Job 1:9–11). Behind the hostility Peter’s readers faced from neighbors and authorities stood a personal enemy of God and His people.

This is the only place in the letter where Peter names the devil, yet the whole letter has described the conflict. The great controversy between Christ and Satan, which began in heaven and continues on earth, takes concrete shape in the pressures of daily life. Satan works through slander, intimidation, temptation, and the weariness that makes believers want to give up. Peter does not speculate about the details of the evil realm. He simply warns that the enemy is real, active, and dangerous, and that his intent is destruction.

He walks about “as a roaring lion.” Lions roar to terrify, and terror scatters sheep, separating the weak from the flock. The image fits the shepherd language of verses 1–4. Persecution and fear can drive believers away from Christ and from one another, and an isolated believer is easy prey. Job 1:7 pictures Satan going to and fro in the earth; Psalm 22:13 uses the roaring lion for the enemies who surrounded the Sufferer. The devil is “seeking whom he may devour,” looking for those he can swallow up through apostasy.

Yet the lion is not all-powerful. He prowls, but the Chief Shepherd has already defeated him at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and his time is short (Revelation 12:12). Watchfulness is the believer’s part; protection is God’s.

wordNotes.term: νήψατε, γρηγορήσατε (nēpsate, grēgorēsate) — be sober, be vigilant
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb describes a clear and self-controlled mind; the second, staying awake and on the alert. Together they call for spiritual readiness. The second verb is the one Jesus used in Gethsemane when He told Peter and the others to watch and pray, and in His teaching about readiness for His return.

wordNotes.term: ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος (ho antidikos hymōn diabolos) — your adversary the devil
wordNotes.explanation: Antidikos was used of an opponent in court; diabolos means slanderer. The pairing presents Satan as an accuser who opposes God’s people and misrepresents both them and God. Scripture identifies him with the ancient serpent and shows his defeat by Christ.

verses.bibleText: Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Whom resist stedfast in the faith.” Peter does not tell believers to flee the lion or to fight it in their own strength. They are to stand their ground against it. The verb means to take a stand and hold one’s position, the same word James uses: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Resistance here is firm refusal to abandon Christ, whatever the pressure.

That firmness comes “in the faith.” The word for steadfast describes something solid and hard, like a foundation that will not shift. Believers stand firm by trusting God and by holding fast to the truth they have received. Personal trust and the shared content of the gospel cannot be separated here; those grounded in the truth are able to keep trusting when the roar grows loud. Paul’s picture of the armor of God makes a similar point, with the shield of faith quenching the fiery darts of the wicked one (Ephesians 6:16).

Peter adds a word of solidarity: “knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.” Suffering tends to isolate, persuading its victims that no one else understands. Believers in Asia Minor were not alone. The worldwide brotherhood was paying the same cost of discipleship. The verb “accomplished” may carry the sense of paying a debt in full, as if each generation of believers bears its share. Knowing this does not lessen the pain, but it removes the lie that their trial was unique or a sign of God’s abandonment.

wordNotes.term: ἀντίστητε στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει (antistēte stereoi tē pistei) — resist stedfast in the faith
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to stand against or withstand; the adjective describes something firm and solid. Believers are to present an unyielding front to the devil, made strong by faith. The same adjective describes the firm foundation of God that stands sure.

Literally “brotherhood,” the community of believers viewed as one family. Peter has already urged his readers to love the brotherhood (2:17). Here the word reminds scattered believers that they belong to a worldwide family that shares their sufferings.

verses.bibleText: But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the God of all grace.” The word “but” sets God over against the adversary of verses 8–9. The lion prowls, seeking to devour; God stands above him as the source of every kind of grace. Peter has spoken of grace that saves (1:10, 13), grace distributed in spiritual gifts (4:10), and grace given to the humble (5:5). All of it flows from one God, and none of it is lacking for those who trust Him.

This God “hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus.” The calling began when the gospel reached Peter’s readers and summoned them out of darkness into light (2:9). Its destination is glory, the same glory Peter mentioned in verses 1 and 4, and it comes “by” or “in” Christ, through union with the One who suffered and was glorified. Because the call comes from God, its goal is secure. He does not summon people to a destiny He cannot bring them to.

“After that ye have suffered a while.” Peter does not hide the suffering. It is real, and it must be passed through. Yet it lasts only “a while,” a short season measured against eternal glory. The letter opened on the same note: “though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations” (1:6). Trials that feel endless are brief when set beside the age to come.

Then comes a cluster of four verbs, each describing what God Himself will do. He will “make you perfect,” restoring and equipping, as fishermen mend nets for use. He will “stablish,” fixing believers firmly so they do not waver. He will “strengthen,” supplying the power they lack. He will “settle,” laying a foundation beneath them, a word that recalls the spiritual house built on Christ (2:5–6). The verbs reach toward the final completion at Christ’s return, when God sets everything right. Yet that work has already begun. The same God who will finish the building is laying stones now, using even suffering to mature and steady His people. Perfection in this sense is completeness and fitness for God’s purpose, a work of grace from first to last.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to put in order, restore, or equip. It is used for mending nets (Mark 1:19) and for restoring a fallen brother (Galatians 6:1), and elsewhere for equipping believers for service. God will make His suffering people whole and fully fitted for His purpose.

To lay a foundation, and so to make firm and stable. The word ties into the letter’s building imagery, where believers are living stones built on Christ. God will ground His people so firmly that no storm can move them.

verses.bibleText: To him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“To him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.” The promise of verse 10 rises naturally into praise. Peter has already offered a similar doxology in 4:11, and here he repeats its central affirmation: dominion belongs to God. Some manuscripts read only “dominion,” which sharpens the point. The word speaks of mighty power and rule.

For believers living under the shadow of Rome, it must often have seemed that dominion belonged to the empire. Rome’s armies, courts, and magistrates held the power of life and death. Peter declares otherwise. The same mighty hand under which believers humble themselves (v. 6) holds dominion forever, and neither the devil nor any earthly ruler can overturn it. Daniel saw the same truth in vision: kingdoms rise and fall, but to the Son of man is given a dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:14). Placed here, after the warning about the devil and the promise of restoration, the doxology reminds suffering believers whose side holds the future. “Amen” seals the confession; it is true, and the church agrees.

wordNotes.explanation: Might or ruling power. The noun is related to the adjective “mighty” in verse 6. Peter ascribes to God the power that governs all things and endures forever, which assures believers that their oppressors do not have the final word.

verses.bibleText: By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly, exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly.” Silvanus is almost certainly the Silas of Acts, a leader of the Jerusalem church who carried the apostles’ decree to Antioch (Acts 15:22–23) and later traveled with Paul through Macedonia and Achaia. He shared imprisonment at Philippi (Acts 16:25) and helped found the church at Thessalonica. Now he serves Peter. The phrase “by Silvanus” in ancient letters often identified the person who delivered a letter; Silvanus may also have helped in its writing. Either way, Peter commends him warmly. The words “as I suppose” express Peter’s settled judgment rather than doubt: he regards Silvanus as a faithful brother and wants the churches to receive him as such.

“Briefly” may seem an odd description of a five-chapter letter, but Peter had far more to say than he could put in writing. Silvanus could add by word of mouth what the page did not hold.

Peter then states the purpose of the whole letter: “exhorting, and testifying that this is the true grace of God wherein ye stand.” He has urged and encouraged, and he has borne witness. What he has described, including the call to suffer for doing good, is the true grace of God. Hardship had not removed his readers from grace; it was part of their life within it. The best manuscripts read the final words as a command: “stand fast in it.” Having heard the truth, they are to plant their feet there and not be moved.

wordNotes.explanation: The fuller Latin form of the name Silas. He was a prophet and leader in the Jerusalem church, a Roman citizen, and Paul’s companion on his second missionary journey. His presence with Peter shows the close bond among the apostolic workers.

wordNotes.term: ἀληθῆ χάριν τοῦ θεοῦ (alēthē charin tou theou) — the true grace of God
wordNotes.explanation: Peter sums up his message as the real, trustworthy grace of God. The adjective guards against any suspicion that suffering means the readers had left God’s favor. Grace in this letter includes both salvation and the strength to endure, received now and fully given at Christ’s revelation.

verses.bibleText: The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you; and so doth Marcus my son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The church that is at Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you.” The Greek says literally “she who is in Babylon, co-elect,” and the word “church” has been supplied to clarify the sense. A few have thought Peter meant his wife, who traveled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5), but the parallel with the greeting at the head of the letter favors a congregation. The readers are the elect sojourners of the dispersion (1:1–2); the church with Peter is elect together with them. John likewise speaks of churches as an elect lady and her children (2 John 1:1, 13).

There is no evidence that Peter ever worked in the city of Babylon on the Euphrates, which was largely deserted by his time. Early Christian tradition places his last labors and death in Rome, and Babylon became a common name for Rome among early believers (Revelation 14:8; 17:5; 18:2). The name carries meaning beyond geography. Babylon was the place of Israel’s exile, the city of proud power that carried God’s people away from Zion. By using it Peter places himself in exile alongside his readers. The capital of the world was, for believers, a foreign land. The later visions of Revelation develop the same name into a symbol of the whole system of opposition to God, which will finally fall.

“And so doth Marcus my son.” This is John Mark, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the church (Acts 12:12). He had once turned back from Paul’s first journey, causing a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Later Paul counted him profitable for ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter calls him “my son,” a term of spiritual affection for a younger coworker, as Paul spoke of Timothy. Early tradition linked Mark’s Gospel with Peter’s preaching. His presence at the close of a letter about steadfastness is itself encouraging: one who had faltered was restored and now stood firm. Peter, who had denied his Lord and been restored by the lakeside, understood that story from the inside.

wordNotes.explanation: Most naturally a symbolic name for Rome, where Peter lived near the end of his life. The name recalls the Babylonian exile and pairs with “the dispersion” in 1:1, presenting the whole church as living away from its true home. Later Scripture uses Babylon for organized opposition to God.

“Chosen together with.” The church in Babylon shares the same election as the believers of Asia Minor. Election in this letter is according to the foreknowledge of God and is realized through the Spirit’s sanctifying work and obedience to Christ.

verses.bibleText: Greet ye one another with a kiss of charity. Peace be with you all that are in Christ Jesus. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Greet ye one another with a kiss of charity.” A kiss on the cheek was a common greeting among family members and close friends in the ancient world. Paul speaks of a “holy kiss” (Romans 16:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:26); Peter calls it a “kiss of charity,” a kiss of love. The gesture declared that believers from different households, backgrounds, and social ranks were now one family. For people rejected by relatives and neighbors, that acceptance mattered greatly. Peter has repeatedly urged love for one another (1:22; 3:8; 4:8), and his last instruction makes that love visible.

“Peace be with you all that are in Christ Jesus. Amen.” The letter that began with a prayer for multiplied grace and peace (1:2) ends with peace. It is the peace Jesus left to His disciples, unlike anything the world gives (John 14:27). It belongs to those “in Christ,” whose lives are joined to Him, and it holds firm even while the lion roars.

wordNotes.term: φιλήματι ἀγάπης (philēmati agapēs) — a kiss of charity
wordNotes.explanation: A greeting expressing family affection among believers. Peter’s phrase links the gesture with agapē, the self-giving love he has urged throughout the letter. It marked the church as a household where strangers were welcomed as kin.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What kind of leadership and what kind of fellowship does a suffering church need in order to stay faithful?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Under the Chief Shepherd, leaders serve willingly and by example, the whole church wears humility, and every believer stands watchful against the adversary while resting in the God of all grace.
discussionQuestions: What three contrasts does Peter use to describe faithful shepherding, and why does each matter in a time of pressure?
How does mutual humility among believers relate to humbling ourselves under God’s mighty hand?
Why does Peter place the command to cast our care on God right before the warning about the roaring lion?
What difference does it make to know that believers elsewhere suffer the same afflictions?
How do the four verbs of verse 10 describe what God does for those who suffer for Christ?
commonMisunderstandings: Peter’s call to submit does not grant leaders unchecked control; elders themselves are forbidden to lord it over the flock.
Humility is not self-contempt; it is the honest posture of a creature who trusts God to lift him up in due time.
Casting care on God does not mean pretending to feel no grief; it means handing the burden to One who cares.
The crown of glory is not received at death but when the Chief Shepherd appears at His return.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep Christ the Chief Shepherd at the center: He models the leadership elders imitate, He will reward them at His appearing, and through Him the God of all grace keeps the flock against the adversary.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Lay down pride and anxiety together under God’s mighty hand, stand firm in the faith against the enemy, and trust the God of all grace to finish what He has begun in you.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: In the conflict between Christ and Satan, the God of all grace calls people to eternal glory in Christ and keeps those who humbly trust Him until the Chief Shepherd appears.
flow: A real adversary seeks to destroy human beings and separate them from God.
Christ, the Good and Chief Shepherd, laid down His life for the sheep and now gathers them.
God resists pride but gives grace to those who humble themselves before Him.
Those who come to Him may cast every care upon Him and stand firm in the faith.
When the Chief Shepherd appears, He will bring His people into eternal glory.
simpleIllustrations: A shepherd who hears a lion at night does not sleep; he gathers the flock close. Christ calls us to stay near Him and near His people.
A heavy load is not handled by worrying over it but by placing it on stronger shoulders; God asks us to hand Him the whole weight.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you humble yourself under God’s mighty hand today and trust the Chief Shepherd to keep you until He appears?
cautions: Do not use the devil as an explanation that removes personal responsibility for sin.
Do not promise that faithfulness will end suffering immediately; Peter speaks of glory after a little while.
Do not present church leaders as owners of the flock; the flock belongs to God.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to serve out of obligation, gain, or control rather than willing love?
Which anxiety am I still holding that I need to place in God’s hands today?
In what areas of my life have I grown careless about the enemy’s strategies?
How can I stand alongside believers who are suffering in other parts of the world?
What would it look like for me to stand fast in the true grace of God this week?
